objective: Building and managing a change-order process: timing it appropriately in the project lifecycle and designing agile processes for rapid change orders
secondaryObjectives: Evaluating scope changes against core project outcomes, weighing the benefits and downfalls of technology-assisted scope/change-order management
Applying scope-management tools and techniques (value engineering, cost-benefit analysis) to identify and close scope gaps

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the construction project manager for a fictional school district's new middle school. The steel frame is going up; change requests from the district arrive weekly and each takes six weeks to approve.
handover: Change orders need three signatures and a paper form.
The core outcome: a school open for the fall term within the 42 million dollar budget.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the commitments, the work items, the risks and issues, the people's support and the milestones.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each status meeting; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: the district rejects two changes already built; 140 thousand dollars of work must be removed.
Week 3: the board refuses extra funds; work is suspended pending a budget decision.
Week 4: the fire marshal refuses the occupancy certificate; opening slips past the fall term.

procPrompt.title: Six weeks per change
procPrompt.context: Crews wait or build at risk.

choices.label: A tiered process: small changes under 25 thousand dollars approved on site within 48 hours by the owner's representative, larger ones weekly by a change board, all in a shared online log
choices.feedback: A change process sized by value and timed to the work avoids stand-by and risk.

choices.label: Ask signatories to sign faster
choices.feedback: Still six weeks for small items.

choices.label: Tell crews to build changes before approval
choices.feedback: Unapproved work may not be paid or may be rejected.

evalPrompt.title: 1.6 million of changes, 1.1 million left
evalPrompt.context: Not all changes serve the outcome.

choices.label: Evaluate each change against the outcome (open for fall, in budget): approve safety and code items, defer nice-to-haves to a later phase

effects.log: Changes are triaged by the outcome.

choices.feedback: Scope changes are judged by what they do for the core outcome.

choices.label: Approve in the order received until contingency runs out
choices.feedback: Important late items may not be funded.

choices.label: Approve them all and request more budget
choices.feedback: The budget is exceeded and the board must find 500 thousand dollars.

vePrompt.title: A gap and no money
vePrompt.context: Code requires a sprinkler upgrade; contingency is short.

choices.label: Run value engineering: an alternative roof finish with the same performance saves 280 thousand dollars, funding the sprinkler upgrade, with a cost-benefit record

effects.log: The gap is closed within budget.

choices.feedback: Value engineering keeps function at lower cost; cost-benefit analysis documents it.

choices.label: Cut the gym's equipment
choices.feedback: It funds the gap but loses a core function.

choices.label: Defer the sprinkler upgrade
choices.feedback: Without it, the building fails inspection.

reflection.question: Write the change record for the district's board.

parts.label: Process
parts.criteria: Tiered approvals within 48 hours or weekly; online log.
parts.modelAnswer: Changes under 25 thousand dollars are approved on site within 48 hours; larger ones weekly, all in a shared log.

parts.label: Scope
parts.criteria: Triaged against the outcome; value engineering funds the sprinkler.
parts.modelAnswer: Pending changes were triaged against opening in budget; a roof finish alternative saves 280 thousand dollars and funds the sprinkler upgrade.

procHarm.headline: A process that keeps up
procHarm.body: Tiered, timely approvals, never build unapproved.

evalHarm.headline: Judge changes by the outcome
evalHarm.body: Keep the school opening on time and in budget.

veHarm.headline: Value-engineer
veHarm.body: Keep function, cut cost, close the gap.

target.headline: Good: changes managed for the outcome
target.body: A fast change process, outcome-based triage and value engineering.

partly.headline: Done, with gaps
partly.body: Nothing was harmed, but a decision was only partly right, or the record left something out. The criteria say which.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: The record was not written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: A change-order process is sized by value and timed to the work, so small changes clear in days and none are built before approval. Scope changes are evaluated against the project's core outcomes. Value engineering keeps function while cutting cost, closing scope gaps within budget.
